candidate.title: William Lane Craig vs Michael Tooley — Is God Real? (2010)
candidate.label: Divine Reality and Evidential Evil
candidate.sourceNote: Based on the complete public English auto-caption transcript of the March 24, 2010 debate at the University of North Carolina at Charlotte, including both speakers’ audience-question answers. Moderator logistics and audience-question premises are unscored context. Automatic-caption ambiguities are treated conservatively; no direct audio verification was required. Summaries condense the arguments, and quotations preserve short source passages.
candidate.scoringNote: Scores are AI-generated estimates of argumentative performance, rather than judgments about worldview truth; the separate AI Contribution does not affect these scores.
candidate.summary: Craig’s cumulative theistic case confronts Tooley’s probabilistic evil argument, with moral perfection and inductive method ultimately deciding a narrowly stronger con case.

pro.text: they do constitute a powerful cumulative case
pro.context: Craig explains that separate arguments contribute different divine attributes and should be evaluated together rather than as isolated demonstrations.

con.text: no contradiction in the existence of an Infinity of natural numbers
con.context: Tooley answers the subtraction paradox by distinguishing different set operations whose unequal remainders remain mathematically consistent.

pro.words: A finite cosmic past and causal principle support a timeless, immaterial, extraordinarily powerful personal origin of spacetime beyond the physical universe itself.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Craig integrates philosophical objections to an actual infinite past with contemporary cosmological evidence, then carefully limits his causal premise to whatever begins existing and derives several attributes appropriate to a transcendent origin. Principal limitation: Neither the impossibility of an actual temporal infinity nor the interpretation of Big Bang cosmology is established decisively here, and the further transition from an atemporal cause to a personal chooser remains suggestive rather than demonstrative. Live burden: Pro must defend the universe’s absolute beginning and the personal-character inference; con may defeat this move by exposing insufficient support for either bridge without establishing a complete eternal cosmology. Locked score: 76 reflects a structurally ambitious and relevant argument whose evidential premises and final agency bridge remain substantially contestable.

con.words: An intelligent immaterial cosmic cause need not be omnipotent, omniscient or good, leaving Craig’s creator arguments short of Tooley’s God, as defined for the central dispute.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Tooley precisely distinguishes existential conclusions about a designer or first cause from the fuller attribute package at issue, preventing evidential support for some supernatural intelligence from silently becoming support for a perfectly good classical deity. Principal limitation: The criticism evaluates the first two arguments in isolation and initially underweights Craig’s announced cumulative strategy, under which moral and resurrection arguments are intended to supply attributes absent from cosmology and design. Live burden: Pro must show how the cumulative evidence reaches the required attributes; Tooley’s local objection succeeds if creator evidence alone lacks that entailment, without his proving rival creators equally likely after every argument. Locked score: 87 reflects a decisive local objection to overclaiming from creator evidence, tempered by the need to evaluate the complete cumulative case.

pro.words: Life-permitting constants occupy an independently specified narrow range, making purposive cosmic design more plausible than necessity or undirected chance under the stated explanatory comparison.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Craig clearly organizes the inference around a narrow life-permitting range, the alleged absence of physically necessary values, and an independently recognizable biological specification, thereby presenting design as comparative explanation rather than simple astonishment. Principal limitation: The chance alternative cannot be assessed without a justified probability distribution over possible constants, while dismissing necessity and multiverse selection requires more scientific argument than the compressed presentation supplies. Live burden: Pro must show that design predicts these constants better than developed naturalistic competitors; con can weaken the inference by identifying an unjustified measure or an inadequately excluded rival without proving that fine-tuning has no evidential force. Locked score: 78 recognizes a lucid, cumulative explanatory case with genuine evidential force, tempered by unresolved measure problems and an incompletely defended elimination of alternatives.

con.words: Tooley broadens causation beyond beginnings, arguing that divine states temporally related to creation would require prior causal conditions just as persisting physical states do.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The electron example shows that causal explanation can concern a thing’s state at a time rather than only its coming into existence, directly challenging an artificially narrow causal vocabulary, because continued existence at a time can depend causally on an earlier state without beginning anew. Principal limitation: From some persisting states having prior causes it does not follow that every temporal state needs a cause, and the claim that causing time places God within it is asserted rather than established. Live burden: Con must justify the unrestricted principle and its applicability to a transcendent agent without generating regress, while pro must explain divine causal activity consistently with timelessness. Locked score: 71 credits an explanatory challenge but records weak generalization from the physical analogy and a weak temporal-location premise.

pro.words: Craig adopts a familiar minimal creator definition and argues that separate lines of evidence cumulatively add moral and revelatory attributes through mutually reinforcing explanatory routes.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Craig explicitly explains the cumulative architecture: cosmology and fine-tuning contribute a powerful personal creator, while moral and resurrection arguments are meant to supplement properties no single inference could establish alone. Principal limitation: Calling the minimal creator God does not resolve Tooley’s announced perfect-goodness target, and Craig rhetorically portrays Tooley as granting the complete cumulative profile although the concessions concern narrower conditional conclusions. Live burden: Pro must establish convergence on one morally perfect agent without shifting definitions, while con must evaluate the combined evidence rather than repeatedly isolating each component. Locked score: 81 credits a coherent response to the attribute-gap objection and an ordinary creator concept, while preserving the unresolved classical-definition dispute and contested premises.

con.words: Standard infinite sets yield different remainders under different subtractions without contradiction, undermining Craig’s arithmetic objection to an infinite past or an actually infinite temporal series.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Tooley’s natural-number examples decisively clarify that infinity minus infinity has no single context-free result, because removing even numbers and removing everything above four are different set operations with perfectly consistent outcomes. Principal limitation: Refuting this subtraction illustration does not by itself establish that a concrete infinite temporal sequence is metaphysically possible or answer other traversal and successive-addition arguments Craig associates with the past. Live burden: This local con reply succeeds by showing that Craig’s subtraction results are mathematically consistent; any stronger con claim about a realized infinite past would require further support, while pro must offer a different contradiction. Locked score: 88 recognizes an exceptionally clear and mathematically grounded rebuttal, limited only in its reach beyond the targeted example.

pro.words: Craig’s causal principle concerns beginnings, allowing an eternal divine cause while requiring explanation for a universe that scientific and philosophical evidence indicates began.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Craig clarifies that his causal premise quantifies over entities with beginnings, and his comparison with the traditional atheist view of an eternal universe shows that the restriction was not invented solely to exempt God. Principal limitation: Blocking a verbal regress does not establish that God is eternal, that the universe began absolutely, or that a beginning requires the kind of personal cause proposed or answer Tooley’s later demand for causes of temporally located divine states. Live burden: Pro must defend the universe’s beginning and divine eternality, while con must challenge those premises rather than misstate the causal rule as applying indiscriminately to everything. Locked score: 85 rewards a precise, fair, and highly responsive answer, with remaining uncertainty located in the cosmological premises rather than the regress objection itself.

pro.words: Craig challenges Tooley’s precise probability result as an artifact of controversial assumptions and arbitrary formal-language choices, when applied to concrete moral evidence.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Craig identifies the exact inferential hinge rather than disputing the emotional salience of suffering, arguing that an objective greater-than-one-half conclusion cannot rest on probability assignments that vary with arbitrary representational decisions. Principal limitation: Reporting that specialists reject a framework and that alternatives exist is partly an appeal to authority, because the response initially gives neither a worked countermodel nor a precise diagnosis of Tooley’s theorem. Live burden: Pro must exhibit a coherent ignorance model that preserves induction while blocking equiprobability, whereas con must show that its assignments remain invariant under redescriptions and property partitions. Locked score: 75 reflects sharp engagement with the central probabilistic premise but also the incomplete in-debate substantiation of the methodological criticism at this stage.

tags.label: Appeal to authority
tags.context: Craig invokes near-universal specialist rejection of Tooley’s probability framework before demonstrating its decisive technical failure.

con.words: Symmetric unknown right- and wrong-making properties allegedly make continued overall wrongness more probable, increasingly so across numerous evils considered across independent catastrophic permissions.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Tooley does not merely appeal to intuition about horrendous suffering; he supplies an explicit four-case model showing how symmetric unknown additions can leave an already negative known balance wrong in three modeled outcomes. Principal limitation: The generalization assumes equal probabilities, comparable weights, independence, and an exhaustive property partition, none of which is secured by the simple illustration and each of which may fail for purposive divine action. Live burden: Con must defend the probability model’s application to morally structured events, while pro must explain which assumption fails and offer a nonarbitrary alternative treatment of ignorance. Locked score: 74 acknowledges valuable formal transparency and cumulative ambition but reflects substantial uncertainty about whether the illustrative theorem represents the real evidential situation.

pro.words: A harmful feature may change moral significance within a larger action, so isolated-property addition can misclassify permission before context is known about the full action and its purpose.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Craig’s heart-surgery example vividly distinguishes an event’s bad experiential feature from its all-things-considered wrongness and shows why contextual explanation can transform moral classification rather than merely add compensating goodness. Principal limitation: Surgical pain comes with an independently verified therapeutic mechanism and consent-sensitive practice, whereas no comparably specific mechanism is established for earthquakes, animal suffering, or hiddenness, so the analogy mainly demonstrates possibility. Live burden: Pro must supply reasons that relevant divine contexts are plausible for actual cases, while con must justify treating visible wrong-making features as probabilistically representative despite missing context. Locked score: 84 rewards a clear conceptual correction with direct force against simple moral arithmetic, while preserving the evidential demand for case-specific justification.

con.words: Tooley assigns equal initial probabilities to good, indifferent, and evil designers, limiting perfect goodness to at most one-third before additional moral evidence is considered.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Tooley identifies neglected moral-character alternatives and insists that evidence for intelligence or power does not automatically discriminate among goodness, indifference, and malevolence, directly pressuring Craig’s attribute bridge. Principal limitation: Equal probability does not follow merely from listing three incompatible predicates, because the partition may be nonexhaustive, differently granular descriptions produce different assignments, and background moral evidence could break symmetry. Live burden: Con must justify a representation-invariant prior over creator characters, while pro must supply positive evidence favoring goodness rather than only rejecting equiprobability. Locked score: 69 credits the important alternative-hypothesis challenge and its motion relevance but reflects that the precise one-third ceiling rests on an insufficiently defended indifference principle.

pro.words: The colored-marble example shows that complete ignorance warrants broad probability intervals rather than precise equal assignments to selected alternatives within arbitrarily redescribed possibility spaces.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Craig presents a concrete partition problem: assigning one-half to red versus nonred conflicts with analogous assignments to blue and green, sharply demonstrating that symmetry of ignorance does not entail a unique precise probability. Principal limitation: The example refutes a naive binary rule more directly than Tooley’s family-of-properties principle, and Craig does not fully establish that the moral-character partition shares every defect of arbitrary color redescriptions. Live burden: Pro must connect interval probability rigorously to the competing creator hypotheses, while con must explain why its good-indifferent-evil categories possess privileged symmetry unavailable to alternative partitions. Locked score: 89 rewards a powerful, lucid counterexample that seriously undermines exact priors, with only the transfer from marbles to moral properties requiring further defense.

con.words: Tooley maintains that his equal-probability principle underwrites justified induction generally, so abandoning it invites sweeping skepticism about unobserved cases and properties.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Tooley recognizes that Craig’s objection threatens the inferential engine of his case and responds at the methodological level, explicitly challenging Craig to provide a viable account of induction rather than merely reject precise assignments. Principal limitation: The claim that this principle is indispensable to induction is largely asserted through references to formal work and philosophical agreement, without showing why interval, comparative, or other Bayesian approaches fail or answering the marble partition counterexample. Live burden: Con must demonstrate indispensability and representation invariance, while pro must supply an alternative that licenses ordinary induction without Tooley’s exact priors. Locked score: 73 credits direct engagement and awareness of the broader epistemic stakes but reflects reliance on authority and insufficient in-debate demonstration.

tags.label: Appeal to authority
tags.context: Tooley invokes Richard Swinburne’s agreement and alleged expertise to bolster his disputed equiprobability principle.

pro.words: Craig offers interval-based robust Bayesian inference as a non-skeptical alternative to Tooley’s precise equiprobability assignments while preserving ordinary inductive reasoning.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Craig finally supplies the requested alternative rather than merely rejecting Tooley’s method, identifying an interval framework that represents complete ignorance without arbitrary exact priors and can still support disciplined inductive learning. Principal limitation: The named marble model is not worked through for morally structured divine permissions, and appeals to specialist opinion do not establish that interval inference preserves every ordinary induction while defeating Tooley’s conclusion. Live burden: Pro must demonstrate the framework’s application to the evil evidence, while con must show why justified induction specifically requires the discarded precise assignments. Locked score: 82 credits a concrete and highly responsive methodological alternative that weakens Tooley’s indispensability claim, moderated by compressed technical exposition and incomplete case-specific derivation.

pro.words: Objective moral experience and naturalism’s evolutionary explanation are used to infer a divine ground for binding values and duties that natural selection cannot supply.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Craig separates an evolutionary explanation of why humans hold moral beliefs from an account of why any moral judgment is objectively true, and he anchors the abstract issue in compelling examples of cruelty. Principal limitation: Showing that evolutionary genealogy does not itself ground moral truth does not eliminate secular realism, constructivism, or other nontheological accounts, so the indispensable divine-ground premise receives less defense than the experiential premise. Live burden: Pro must demonstrate that objective normativity specifically requires personal divine authority; because Tooley affirmatively invokes secular realism, his positive alternative gains force only insofar as at least one such account is substantively credible. Locked score: 74 rewards the argument’s intuitive moral data and clear syllogistic relevance but registers the unsupported exclusivity claim at its decisive inferential step.

con.words: Parallel ontological arguments allegedly yield incompatible necessary beings, so Tooley declares necessary temporal personhood incoherent and unusable for moral grounding across every metaphysically possible world.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Tooley uses vivid parody cases to expose how an unrestricted possibility-to-necessity pattern could license mutually incompatible conclusions, correctly warning that no valid method can establish contradictory necessary beings. Principal limitation: Refuting a particular ontological inference does not establish that every necessarily existing nonabstract person is contradictory, because the relevant possibility premises may differ and no contradiction in necessary personhood itself is derived. Live burden: Con must prove the modal impossibility it later needs for moral truth, while pro need only distinguish coherent divine necessity from the unsupported parody possibilities. Locked score: 55 reflects the argument’s understandable diagnostic force against careless ontological reasoning but marks its major non sequitur from invalid proof to metaphysical impossibility.

pro.words: Different authorities possess different permissions, so divine authorship of life may affect whether permitting death or suffering is wrongful within morally significant creator-creature relationships.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: The mother-and-stranger comparison gives concrete support for agent-relative permission: identical conduct can receive different moral evaluation when authority, responsibility, and an established relationship differ between the actors. Principal limitation: Limited parental authority does not establish unlimited divine prerogative, and being life’s source does not independently show permission to impose any suffering regardless of necessity, compassion, proportionality, or creatures’ claims. Live burden: Pro must explain the principled scope and moral constraints of divine authority, while con must establish why relevant creator-creature differences cannot alter the applicable duty. Locked score: 74 credits an important challenge to Tooley’s agent-neutral premise but reflects the analogy’s inability by itself to justify the disputed divine permissions.

con.words: Live secular realist theories prevent Craig from assuming that objective value is impossible without theological grounding until those competitors receive substantive examination.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Tooley correctly places the burden on a universal impossibility claim and names multiple developed nontheological accounts, showing that an evolutionary debunking story does not exhaust the philosophical alternatives to divine morality. Principal limitation: Listing philosophers and books establishes disagreement rather than truth, and the move does not explain how any selected theory grounds normativity, intrinsic value, or authoritative duties better than Craig’s proposal. Live burden: Pro must engage the strongest secular account before claiming exclusivity, while con must articulate at least one account sufficiently to demonstrate genuine explanatory viability rather than relying on scholarly existence. Locked score: 83 recognizes excellent burden placement and responsiveness to the moral syllogism, tempered by the absence of substantive defense for the cited alternatives.

pro.words: If divine prohibition constitutes wrongness, condemning an event God permits may presuppose the falsity of Craig’s command-based moral theory before that competing theory is assessed.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Craig raises a relevant grounding challenge by asking whether Tooley’s judgment of divine permission relies on a moral standard that still requires defense within the wider dispute over objective normativity. Principal limitation: He does not establish that Tooley’s independent wrong-making premise begs the question, and his reply becomes circular if God’s goodness is inferred from the permissions whose moral status is disputed. Live burden: Pro must ground goodness independently of those permissions and explain its constraint on divine action; con need only defend the moral premises actually used against the command account, not construct a complete external system. Locked score: 61 reflects a pertinent challenge to moral grounding but also insufficient engagement with Tooley’s premise, serious circularity risk, and failure to protect creatures against divine harm.

con.words: Because basic moral truths hold necessarily, Tooley argues they remain true in Godless possible worlds and cannot depend exclusively on God, as their sole ontological truth-maker.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Tooley constructs a modal dilemma in which contingent divine states cannot ground truths holding in every possible world, while necessary divine existence faces his separate objection to necessary temporal personhood. Principal limitation: The second branch inherits the unsupported leap from unsuccessful ontological arguments to the impossibility of a necessary person, and the first branch cannot engage a theist who coherently treats God as necessary. Live burden: Con must establish that necessary divine personhood is impossible or explain moral necessity without assuming God’s contingency, while pro must articulate how divine nature grounds truths across possible worlds. Locked score: 72 credits a relevant modal challenge but reflects its decisive dependence on a weak earlier impossibility premise rather than any demonstrated failure in the contingent-world reasoning alone.

pro.words: Craig argues that secular realism posits objective values without explaining their authority, especially the obligation to follow virtues over vices within a thoroughly naturalistic ontology.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Craig distinguishes abstract moral values from authoritative obligations and asks why agents must align with kindness rather than greed, thereby focusing the dispute on practical normativity instead of merely cataloguing valuable and vicious properties. Principal limitation: He does not engage the secular accounts Tooley names, and his claim that obligation requires a commander remains unsupported against proposals grounded in reasons, welfare, relationships, or rational agency. Live burden: Pro must demonstrate the necessity and explanatory superiority of divine authority; because Tooley affirmatively invokes secular realism, his alternative gains force when at least one such account is substantively credible. Locked score: 79 recognizes serious engagement with moral grounding and a pointed obligations challenge, moderated by the failure to exclude nontheological explanations.

con.words: If commands bind only creatures and God issues none to himself, command-based morality leaves divine infliction of suffering unconstrained toward sentient creatures with intrinsic interests.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Tooley targets the theory’s internal structure rather than merely reiterating moral outrage, showing that commands addressed to persons cannot by themselves explain why God’s own treatment of sentient creatures would be objectively limited. Principal limitation: Calling the result moral nihilism overstates the conclusion because the theory still governs creaturely conduct, and Craig can supplement commands with constraints derived from an essentially good divine nature. Live burden: The local con objection succeeds against a command-only account if divine action remains unconstrained; if con also challenges Craig’s later nature-based supplement, its evidence must address how compassion and fairness apply to disputed permissions. Locked score: 83 rewards a powerful divine-exemption objection central to evil and moral grounding, moderated by its rhetorical overreach and an available nature-based reply.

pro.words: Natural and moral suffering may be necessary background for maximizing freely chosen knowledge of God rather than earthly happiness within a providential history extending beyond death.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Craig supplies a definite higher-order purpose—freely formed relationship with God—and correctly observes that judging gratuitousness requires comparison with feasible worlds, including their long-range consequences for agency, character, and salvation. Principal limitation: The possibility that suffering contributes to optimal salvation does not establish that actual quantities, victims, or distributions are necessary, and the asserted optimization remains unsupported by comparative evidence available within the debate. Live burden: Pro must connect particular severe evils to plausible constraints on freer or less harmful worlds, while con must avoid assuming that any unseen purpose is absent simply because observers cannot identify it. Locked score: 75 recognizes a relevant undercutting explanation with real modal force, while withholding stronger credit because optimality and proportionality are asserted rather than demonstrated.

con.words: Extensive natural, moral, animal, and bodily suffering joins hiddenness and conditional scriptural horrors as evidence against perfect goodness across human history and religious traditions.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Tooley assembles diverse kinds of suffering while carefully marking claims about biblical violence and hell as conditional upon scriptural truth, which preserves the argument against both secular and Christian responses without confusing their evidential status. Principal limitation: A broad catalogue establishes severity and variety but does not yet demonstrate gratuitousness, and several cases require separate analysis because natural suffering, human wrongdoing, hiddenness, and alleged revelation invite importantly different explanations. Live burden: Con must connect representative cases to the probabilistic inference that adequate divine reasons are unlikely, while pro must address the actual distribution rather than offering only abstract logical possibilities. Locked score: 81 reflects substantial evidential breadth and commendable conditional precision, offset by the preliminary nature of the catalogue before its inferential bridge is supplied.

pro.words: Widespread human wrongdoing fits Christianity’s expectation of rebellion, guilt, alienation, and consequent need for divine forgiveness within the Christian diagnosis of humanity.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Craig situates moral evil within a recognizable Christian account of misused freedom and alienation, so the prevalence of wrongdoing is not automatically surprising if that worldview is already under consideration. Principal limitation: Predicting rebellion after adopting Christianity offers limited independent confirmation, and the response does not explain why an omnipotent creator permits extreme harms, structures freedom with these risks, or fails to restrain perpetrators more often. Live burden: Pro must show that morally significant freedom plausibly requires this scale of preventable suffering, while con must distinguish evidence against God from evil directly produced by finite agents. Locked score: 69 credits worldview coherence and relevance to moral evil but reflects weak comparative prediction and an incomplete answer to divine permission.

con.words: Known severe wrong-making features without visible counterweights support a probabilistic inference that some divine permissions are wrong overall, all things considered under complete information.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Tooley formulates the evidential problem as a transparent sequence from observed wrong-making features through all-things-considered wrongness to incompatibility with perfect goodness, avoiding the easily rebutted claim that suffering logically contradicts any deity. Principal limitation: The decisive transition from no known adequate reason to probable absence of an adequate reason depends on the contested treatment of unknown properties and on whether human observers should expect epistemic access to divine purposes. Live burden: Con must justify that known evidence reliably tracks the complete moral balance, while pro must provide a principled reason for withholding the inference without collapsing into unrestricted skepticism. Locked score: 86 rewards a rigorous, motion-focused probabilistic structure whose most important known-to-unknown premise remains the central unresolved controversy.

pro.words: Incomparable eternal joy may compensate finite suffering, making earthly anguish small relative to a person’s entire existence under the promised Christian afterlife.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Craig appropriately widens the evaluative horizon beyond earthly life and identifies compensation as morally relevant when the hypothesis itself includes resurrection, restoration, and unending flourishing for sufferers. Principal limitation: Compensation after harm is not automatically justification for permitting preventable harm, and the response neither establishes universal access to eternal joy nor shows that an infinite benefit licenses every finite means. Live burden: Pro must distinguish making victims whole from furnishing a sufficient permission before suffering occurs, while con must assess the theistic afterlife conditionally rather than excluding it at the outset. Locked score: 72 recognizes that eternity materially changes aggregate welfare calculations but marks the unresolved moral gap between eventual compensation, proportional permission, and equitable salvation.

con.words: Unrelated goods do not answer whether particular catastrophic permissions lack sufficient reasons, and symmetric unknowns preserve probable wrongness regarding that permission all things considered.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Tooley distinguishes global quantities of good from morally sufficient reasons for permitting a particular disaster, and the parallel argument against a perfectly evil being clarifies why unrelated benefits do not simply cancel local evidence. Principal limitation: The renewed greater-than-one-half conclusion still inherits contested assumptions about equal and independent unknown right- and wrong-making properties, while dismissing divine authority rhetorically does not answer Craig’s nature-constrained version. Live burden: Con must justify the probabilistic calculation for specific permissions, while pro must identify plausible counterbalancing relations rather than pointing generically to goodness elsewhere. Locked score: 81 credits a valuable clarification of evidential scope and all-things-considered judgment, tempered by continued dependence on the disputed probability framework.

pro.words: Craig cites reported post-earthquake conversions in Haiti as a possible salvific consequence that could help justify divine permission despite the disaster’s immense temporal harms.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Craig moves beyond wholly abstract possibility by connecting his optimal-salvation theodicy to the focal Haitian disaster and offering a concrete report of extensive religious response after the earthquake. Principal limitation: A single missionary email supplies no independent verification, baseline, casualty comparison, or causal evidence, and post-disaster conversion neither proves divine intention nor establishes that comparable salvation required catastrophic suffering. Live burden: Pro must corroborate the report and show necessity, proportionality, and victim-sensitive benefit, while con must allow that genuine salvific consequences could count morally without treating temporal sequence as justification. Locked score: 69 recognizes direct responsiveness and a specific proposed purpose but reflects exceptionally weak empirical support and a large inferential gap from aftermath to permission.

con.words: An irrevocable hell seems inconsistent with perfect goodness because a loving creator could preserve opportunities for repentance and return after death without arbitrary temporal closure.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The prodigal-child comparison gives Tooley’s objection a clear moral standard of continuing openness to reconciliation, focusing attention on whether permanent closure expresses perfect love even after an initially free rejection. Principal limitation: The argument assumes a permanently locked conception of hell and does not engage accounts on which character becomes fixed, postmortem choice remains meaningful, punishment serves justice, or scriptural language describes final separation differently, leaving the assumed no-return doctrine insufficiently defended. Live burden: Con must show that irrevocability is appreciably less expected from perfect goodness, while pro must explain continued closure rather than merely repeat that separation begins voluntarily. Locked score: 84 rewards a precise and responsive evidential refinement of the evil challenge, with limited deduction for doctrinal assumptions.

pro.words: The empty tomb, reported appearances, and transformed resurrection belief are presented as historical facts best explained by divine action within first-century Jewish religious expectations.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Craig offers a compact abductive structure built from three independently intelligible historical claims and emphasizes that an adequate explanation must jointly account for the empty tomb, appearances, and sudden resurrection-centered conviction. Principal limitation: The debate largely treats those facts and the inadequacy of naturalistic explanations as settled, although their evidential independence, source reliability, and comparative likelihoods require substantial defense before resurrection becomes the best explanation. Live burden: Pro must establish the historical data and compare resurrection against serious natural hypotheses; con can block the inference by undermining a pivotal fact or comparative claim without furnishing a complete explanation of the entire cluster. Locked score: 74 reflects a coherent and directly relevant historical argument whose crucial factual establishment and comparative-explanation work remain significantly abbreviated.

tags.label: Appeal to authority
tags.context: Craig treats majority historical consensus and universal scholarly rejection as establishing resurrection facts and excluding natural explanations.

con.words: A genuine resurrection would indicate supernatural action, but identifying its agent as the perfectly good, omnipotent, omniscient God requires further evidence.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Tooley isolates the indispensable identification premise between extraordinary historical agency and the classical divine attributes, preventing the evidential force of an alleged resurrection from silently carrying conclusions about unlimited power, exhaustive knowledge, and perfect goodness. Principal limitation: The objection initially overlooks how a miracle’s historical and religious setting may identify its intended agent and communicate vindication, leaving Craig room to argue from Jesus’ claims, execution, and Israelite context. Live burden: Pro must show that this context supports the defined God beyond an unspecified supernatural cause; con can reasonably question that identification without supplying an equally detailed alternative agent. Locked score: 88 reflects an exceptionally clear correction of inferential overreach that remains answerable through additional contextual evidence.

pro.words: Jesus’ claims, execution for blasphemy, and resurrection context are used to identify the raising agent as Israel’s God rather than an unspecified supernatural power.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Craig locates the alleged miracle within Jesus’ religious self-presentation and execution on a blasphemy charge, giving resurrection a plausible vindicatory meaning within Israel’s religious narrative rather than leaving an anonymous supernatural intervention. Principal limitation: The argument presupposes reliable accounts of Jesus’ claims and does not adequately examine limited, deceptive, or morally ambiguous agents, while identification with Yahweh still leaves perfect goodness and other classical attributes to be defended. Live burden: Pro must establish that the historical context justifies this specific identification; con may weaken that inference by exposing underdetermination or unreliable context without producing an equally probable rival agent. Locked score: 83 credits a direct and historically specific reply to the agent gap but preserves significant evidential and moral-attribute qualifications.

con.words: Negative modern miracle investigations and documented legend growth lower resurrection’s prior plausibility and strengthen natural historical alternatives for the earliest Christian resurrection claims.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Tooley brings comparative empirical considerations to the resurrection debate, combining claimed failures of careful modern miracle investigations with a concrete mechanism by which nonmiraculous narratives can acquire supernatural elements over time. Principal limitation: The cited studies and legend example are summarized without methods, representativeness, or direct linkage to the earliest resurrection sources, and low modern frequency does not independently explain every claimed historical fact. Live burden: Con must show that legend development plausibly accounts for the relevant records and chronology, while pro must establish evidential reliability strong enough to overcome a low miracle prior. Locked score: 81 rewards a coherent, evidence-oriented alternative framework, with reservations about sweeping empirical claims and the absence of a complete naturalistic reconstruction.

pro.words: Immediate personal awareness of God may rationally ground belief without inference, provided its undefeated experiential warrant survives challenges from rival culturally conditioned experiences.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Craig identifies a legitimate epistemic category in which some beliefs are rationally basic rather than inferred, thereby explaining how personal acquaintance could matter even when public arguments remain inconclusive. Principal limitation: The analogy with perception and memory is asserted more than defended, and the account initially lacks criteria distinguishing veridical divine awareness from culturally conditioned, psychologically generated, or mutually incompatible religious experiences. Live burden: Pro must specify reliable markers and answer concrete defeaters, while con must show that disagreement or correlation defeats this claimant’s warrant rather than automatically discrediting every immediate experience. Locked score: 70 credits a philosophically recognizable route to personal justification but reflects its limited public evidential reach and underdeveloped reliability conditions.

tags.label: Subjective validation
tags.context: Craig presents private personal experience of God as immediate knowledge apart from external evidence or argument.

con.words: Conflicting religious experiences and their close dependence on prior formation undermine their reliability as objective divine disclosure rather than products of enculturation.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Tooley offers two distinct defeaters—mutually incompatible experiential contents and strong cultural correlation—and charitably allows initial justification before arguing that later awareness of disagreement can undermine confidence. Principal limitation: Disagreement does not automatically defeat every experience, and the asserted strength of cultural dependence is illustrated through examples rather than systematic evidence or comparison with ordinary perception under disagreement. Live burden: Con must show that these patterns are expected more strongly on psychological formation than genuine revelation, while pro must supply discriminating evidence for Christian experience instead of asserting asymmetric defeaters. Locked score: 84 rewards a clear, directly responsive, and appropriately probabilistic critique, with modest deduction for empirical claims that remain largely undocumented in the exchange.

pro.words: Craig argues that hiddenness may preserve relationship, scriptural atrocities chiefly threaten inerrancy, and hell expresses freely maintained separation within Craig’s broader Christian theodicy.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Craig separates three distinct objections and gives each a tailored reply, especially conceding that biblical moral difficulties could undermine inerrancy without directly disproving God and framing hell through agency rather than imposed torture. Principal limitation: The hiddenness rationale remains speculative, distancing atrocities from God weakens the revelation case, and voluntary entry does not explain why separation must become everlasting or why corrective opportunities cannot continue. Live burden: Pro must show that these policies plausibly express perfect love and preserve freedom, while con must keep conditional scriptural claims distinct from independent evidence against deity. Locked score: 68 credits responsive distinctions and limited concessions but records that the central explanations of hiddenness and irrevocable hell remain substantially underargued.

tags.label: Red herring
tags.context: Craig redirects conditional evidence about Yahweh’s moral character into a separate dispute over biblical inerrancy.

con.words: Conditional on scriptural portrayals, Yahweh’s attributed violence and eternal punishment count against identifying Jesus’ raiser as perfectly good under the debate’s classical definition.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Tooley conditionally accepts Craig’s historical identification and then tests whether the identified agent satisfies the disputed moral attribute, citing concrete portrayals rather than treating the name Yahweh as equivalent to perfect goodness. Principal limitation: The rapid catalogue does not address genre, historical reliability, judgment contexts, progressive revelation, or rival interpretations, and the conclusion that Yahweh is profoundly evil exceeds what these compressed citations independently establish. Live burden: Con must defend the moral and textual reading of representative cases, while pro must reconcile them with essential goodness rather than merely questioning scriptural inerrancy. Locked score: 82 recognizes a direct, evidence-bearing challenge to the identification bridge, with deductions for interpretive compression and excessive moral certainty.

pro.words: Craig grants other believers initial experiential warrant but maintains Christian experience remains rational until a specific defeater succeeds against the live disagreement evidence.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Craig charitably concedes that Muslim experience may provide prima facie justification and distinguishes initial rational warrant from later defeat, avoiding the crude claim that only Christian experiences can ever count evidentially. Principal limitation: He asserts that Islam has defeaters and Christianity lacks them without presenting those reasons, and he does not answer Tooley’s separate cultural-correlation evidence showing that experiential content tracks prior formation. Live burden: Pro must demonstrate why disagreement and correlation do not defeat this Christian experience, while con must show that these facts outweigh the ordinary presumption favoring sincere experience. Locked score: 76 recognizes a coherent defeater framework and commendable concession, with reduced credit for asymmetric, unspecified defeaters and limited public evidential force.

tags.label: Subjective validation
tags.context: Craig treats God’s personal reality in his life as sufficient warrant while the stated cultural-correlation defeater remains unanswered.

con.words: Jesus’ alleged predictive errors, punitive teachings, and acceptance of hell make resurrection by an omniscient and morally perfect being less probable.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Tooley develops an independent conditional test of Craig’s vindication thesis by asking whether an omniscient and perfectly good agent would probably endorse the particular beliefs and moral attitudes attributed to Jesus. Principal limitation: His examples depend on contested interpretations of imminent-return sayings, demonic language, Mosaic law, judgment rhetoric, and hell, yet alternative readings and historical context receive almost no consideration. Live burden: Con must show that these attributions are credible and appreciably less expected if a perfectly good God vindicated Jesus; pro can answer by defending their interpretation or weakening their evidential relevance. Locked score: 76 credits a source-specific probabilistic challenge supported by concrete historical texts but reflects the bundled claims and insufficient interpretive defense.

pro.words: A necessarily existing God may be timeless without creation yet acquire temporal relations upon creating, without contradiction or loss of metaphysical necessity.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Craig cleanly distinguishes metaphysical necessity from temporal mode and offers a coherent model in which an uncreated being exists timelessly sans universe but enters temporal relations with creation. Principal limitation: The response establishes conceptual possibility mainly by noting that Tooley never demonstrated contradiction; it does not explain in depth how a person timeless without creation can stand in temporal relations after creation while remaining metaphysically necessary. Live burden: Pro need only defend coherence against Tooley’s impossibility claim, although a fuller positive account would strengthen the model, while con must derive an actual contradiction rather than rely on analogy with abstract numbers. Locked score: 79 rewards a concise and appropriately limited rebuttal that neutralizes the asserted impossibility, with modest reservation about its undeveloped metaphysics.

con.words: Tooley defines the target as a perfectly good, omniscient, omnipotent personal creator and argues probabilistically from evil against it through observed apparently gratuitous suffering.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Tooley states the target attributes and burden with exceptional discipline, explicitly distinguishing evidential improbability from logical incompatibility and thereby preventing stronger conclusions from being mistakenly demanded of his case. Principal limitation: Defining God classically does not by itself show that every ordinary use of the debate motion carries all those attributes, so the later definitional conflict requires an argument about the intended proposition rather than stipulation alone. Live burden: Con must show that observed suffering appreciably lowers the probability of precisely this perfect being, while pro may defend either compatibility with perfection or a justified broader conception of God. Locked score: 89 recognizes unusually clear burden allocation and conceptual framing, with only a residual motion-definition dispute limiting complete decisiveness.

pro.words: Craig grounds limits on divine willing in God’s essentially good, compassionate, and fair nature rather than self-addressed commands even when no external duties bind God.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Craig answers the self-command problem by distinguishing the source of creaturely duties from the constraints on God, avoiding voluntarism and denying that divine will could reverse love and hatred, because essential compassion and fairness would restrict commands before any discretionary act of willing. Principal limitation: Essential goodness is asserted without an independent criterion, while the claim of broad authority over life leaves unclear how compassion and fairness constrain permissions of catastrophic suffering. Live burden: Pro must make the nature-based standard independently informative enough to evaluate disputed actions, while con may expose circularity or tension between the stated virtues and claimed divine permissions without proving logical inconsistency. Locked score: 80 credits a substantial repair to divine-command theory, balanced against unresolved circularity and the uncertain practical limits of divine prerogative.

con.words: Tooley argues that moving from a perfectly good classical God to a bare creator evades rather than answers his evil case against the originally specified classical target.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Tooley identifies the practical and argumentative difference between a supernatural creator and a perfectly good governor, noting that evidence for an evil creator would not satisfy the religious assurances associated with the classical motion target. Principal limitation: Attributing the shift solely to strategic avoidance overstates motive and underplays Craig’s initial cumulative structure, which openly used distinct arguments to assemble a fuller conception beyond the first two conclusions. Live burden: Con must justify the classical definition from the debate’s motion and assess the cumulative profile, while pro must avoid treating minimal creator evidence as sufficient if perfect goodness remains essential. Locked score: 86 rewards a central, clearly expressed definitional safeguard, with a deduction for motivational rhetoric and incomplete acknowledgment of cumulative intent.

pro.words: Certain divine foreknowledge does not make the known action necessary, because different free action would correspond to different knowledge under the relevant counterfactual dependence.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Craig clearly distinguishes the necessity of a conditional from necessity of its consequent and uses the infallible-barometer analogy to explain how knowledge can track an event without determining it, because a different free act would correspond to different divine knowledge rather than falsified knowledge. Principal limitation: The account establishes a modal distinction but leaves deeper questions about timeless knowledge, counterfactual dependence, and the metaphysics of an already settled future largely outside the exchange. Live burden: Pro must defend compatibility rather than prove foreknowledge itself, while con must identify a contradiction in logical dependence without converting it prematurely into efficient backward causation. Locked score: 89 recognizes exceptionally lucid modal reasoning, direct responsiveness, and careful calibration, with only residual metaphysical questions beyond the specific fatalist inference.

con.words: Tooley contends that making divine knowledge depend on later choices invokes disputed and possibly contradictory backward causation from future action to prior cognition.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Tooley identifies an ambiguity in Craig’s statement that God knows because the event occurs: if that explanatory dependence were causal rather than logical, an account of temporally reversed influence would indeed be required. Principal limitation: Craig explicitly described logical priority rather than efficient causation, so recasting dependence as a later event causing earlier knowledge attacks a stronger claim than the presented account and leaves the modal reply intact within Craig’s explicitly noncausal barometer analogy. Live burden: Con must show that logical dependence entails problematic causation, while pro should clarify the noncausal truth-making or explanatory relation underlying foreknowledge. Locked score: 59 reflects the objection’s relevance to divine coherence but also its misreading, thin support, and failure to engage Craig’s central distinction.

strengths: Craig repeatedly identifies the precise premise under attack and supplies direct replies rather than relying solely on opening assertions.
His marble example gives a vivid, technically relevant reason to distrust exact probabilities manufactured from complete ignorance.
The cumulative structure lets cosmology, fine-tuning, morality, resurrection, and experience contribute distinct features to one theistic hypothesis.
His distinction between certainty and necessity provides the debate’s clearest analysis of foreknowledge and freedom.

blunders.text: Craig sometimes treats unverified or compressed evidence, especially the Haitian missionary report, as carrying much greater justificatory weight than its source supports.
The move from divine ownership of life to broad permission for suffering remains insufficiently reconciled with the compassion and fairness attributed to God.
Several arguments establish at most a creator or supernatural agent before the cumulative bridge to perfect goodness has been independently secured.

strengths: Tooley consistently preserves the distinction between evidential improbability and strict logical incompatibility throughout his argument from evil.
He sharply exposes the gap between evidence for an intelligent creator and evidence for an omniscient, omnipotent, perfectly good God.
His actual-infinity response correctly explains why different infinite-set subtractions do not constitute a mathematical contradiction.
The irrevocability objection to hell directly addresses a feature left unanswered by describing separation as freely chosen.

blunders.text: Tooley’s exact probability assignments depend on symmetry, partition, and independence assumptions that his four-case illustration does not adequately establish.
He moves invalidly from weaknesses in ontological arguments to the sweeping claim that every necessarily existing temporal person is self-contradictory.
His backward-causation objection overlooks Craig’s explicit distinction between logical dependence and efficient causal influence from the future.

finalArgument.thesis: The cumulative evidence favors a necessarily existing personal creator whose good nature grounds normativity and whose purposes can remain partly beyond finite observers.
premises: A temporally finite universe requires an explanation that is not itself contained within physical spacetime.
Fine-tuned life-permitting structure is more expected if the explanatory source can select among physically possible arrangements.
Objective duties are more intelligible if practical authority is grounded in an essentially good personal reality.
Historically situated religious evidence can identify a generic creator more specifically when assessed cumulatively rather than separately.
Finite observers should not infer purposelessness confidently when morally relevant consequences extend across free histories and possible afterlife.
finalArgument.conclusion: Taken together, these considerations make a good personal creator a more unified explanation than unrelated naturalistic accounts of origin, order, normativity, and revelation.

newArguments.title: Cross-Domain Explanatory Unity
newArguments.text: A single personal-source hypothesis can connect otherwise separate explanatory questions: why physical reality begins, why its parameters support agents, why agents encounter categorical moral demands, and why historical religious claims arise. This unity counts only if the connections generate genuine expectations, but it supplies cumulative value unavailable when every domain receives an unrelated stopping point.

newArguments.title: Moral Knowledge Constraint
newArguments.text: If human moral cognition is sufficiently reliable to condemn apparently gratuitous suffering, that same reliability may support the perception that persons possess objective worth and duties. A theistic explanation can treat both judgments as products of rational creatures designed for moral knowledge, while still requiring specific reasons before any particular divine permission is judged justified.

finalArgument.thesis: The world’s suffering and ambiguity fit poorly with a perfectly good, omnipotent, omniscient governor, while Craig’s evidence repeatedly reaches weaker supernatural conclusions.
premises: Numerous severe harms display known wrong-making features without observable reasons proportionate to their victims’ losses.
Perfect power and knowledge would remove ordinary limitations that excuse finite agents from preventing such harms.
Evidence for a cosmic cause or designer does not by itself identify perfect goodness, unlimited power, or omniscience.
Religious experiences and miracle reports vary with prior communities and possess familiar pathways of psychological or legendary development.
A morally perfect revealer would be expected to provide clearer, less culturally dependent access while preserving meaningful freedom.
finalArgument.conclusion: The combined evidence therefore leaves a generic creator possible but makes the classical perfectly good God less credible than Craig’s cumulative rhetoric suggests.

newArguments.title: Distributional Suffering Test
newArguments.text: The evidential challenge strengthens when attention shifts from suffering in general to its distribution among infants, animals, isolated populations, and persons whose anguish produces no visible moral development. A defense based on free relationship should explain why these particular victims and intensities are predictably connected to that end rather than merely compatible with an unknown plan.

newArguments.title: Revelatory Signal Quality
newArguments.text: A perfectly informed and loving revealer could preserve voluntary response while presenting a public signal less dependent on birthplace, inherited doctrine, disputed texts, and private experience. The observed pattern of incompatible traditions resembles noisy human transmission, so hiddenness and religious diversity jointly reduce the likelihood of a universally concerned divine communicator.

noveltyMap.explanation: This synthesis combines five independently presented routes into one conditional explanatory comparison while preserving the unresolved attribute and providence bridges identified during debate.
The debate states cumulative support, but this extension newly formulates cross-domain unification as an evidential virtue constrained by distinct predictive expectations.
This extension connects confidence in evil judgments with confidence in objective human worth, a reflexive constraint implicit but not expressly developed in the exchange.

This synthesis integrates evidential evil, the creator-attribute gap, religious disagreement, and historical transmission into one comparative conclusion without converting probability into contradiction.
The extension develops the debate’s catalogue into a distribution-sensitive test focused on victim selection and intensity rather than simply repeating aggregate suffering.
The extension unifies hiddenness, cultural correlation, and legend growth through a signal-quality expectation that neither speaker explicitly formulated during the debate.
